patient.chief_complaint: Sudden severe headache 1 hour ago, vomiting, now headache 'getting better'
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Davis is a 62-year-old man with known severe anemia (Hgb 7.2 g/dL) and hypertension who presents with sudden onset severe headache 1 hour ago. He was reading when he developed an explosive headache rated 10/10, with immediate nausea and vomiting once. He called his wife who brought him to the ED. The headache has improved to 6/10 with an ice pack. He has mild neck stiffness. The key diagnostic challenge in this case is the severe anemia: a patient with Hgb 7.2 g/dL may have an isodense SAH on non-contrast CT (blood density is proportional to hemoglobin concentration, and with severe anemia, the blood may be isodense to normal brain, making CT less reliable). He denies any prior severe headaches, focal weakness, or loss of consciousness. His last CBC showed Hgb 7.2 g/dL - GI evaluation for iron deficiency was pending when he last saw his PCP. He is not on anticoagulation.

output.summary: Severe anemia reduces CT sensitivity for SAH - subarachnoid blood may appear isodense or hypodense rather than hyperdense. LP with spectrophotometry remains the gold standard. During the vasospasm period, anemia independently worsens outcomes by reducing oxygen delivery to at-risk brain - transfusion threshold in SAH may be more liberal (8-10 g/dL) than standard surgical thresholds.
